narration.full_text: Let's dive into the world of real numbers. A real number is essentially any number that can be placed on a number line, representing continuous quantities like length or temperature. We denote the set of all real numbers with the symbol R. Real numbers are fundamental because they have no gaps; between any two real numbers, you'll find infinitely many others. This completeness is a key property, especially as you advance in mathematics. Now, let's explore how we classify these real numbers into different categories. We'll start with the most basic: natural numbers. These are the positive integers we use for counting, like one, two, three, and so on. Remember, zero is not included in this set. Next, we have whole numbers. This set simply adds zero to the natural numbers. So, whole numbers include zero, one, two, and so forth. All whole numbers are also integers and, by extension, real numbers. Moving on, rational numbers are those that can be expressed as a fraction, p over q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. Their decimal forms either terminate or repeat. For example, negative two-fifths, zero point two, or seven-thirds are all rational numbers. Finally, we have irrational numbers. These are real numbers that cannot be written as a simple fraction. Their decimal representations are non-terminating and non-repeating. Classic examples include the square root of two, the square root of three, and pi. Understanding these classifications is crucial for building a strong mathematical foundation.
